slides.title: Searching

blocks.text: Searching is the process of finding a target element within a group of elements or determine that the target does not exist.
Two common approaches to searching: linear search and binary search.
Our goal is to perform the search as fast as possible.
We should minimize the number of comparisons needed to find the target element.
Binary search is more efficient than linear search, but the elements must be sorted first before searching.

slides.title: Static Methods

blocks.text: A static method (called a class method) is invoked through the class name. It is declared using the static keyword.
For example, all the methods of the Math class are static.
Math.sqrt(x) invokes the static sqrt method in Math.
Static methods cannot access instance variables because they do not operate on a particular object.
Static methods can only invoke other static methods and only access static variables.

slides.title: Binary Search

blocks.text: If the array is sorted, searching an array for a target element can be more efficient than linear search.
Instead of starting at index 0, binary search begins in the middle of the array. If the target is not found, we know that if it is in the array, it is in one half or the other.
We can then jump to the middle of that half and continue.

slides.title: The Comparable Interface

blocks.text: The generic Comparable<T> interface is used to define an ordering of objects of type T.
It is typically used for searching and sorting arrays and lists.
The Comparable<T> interface defines a single method:
int compareTo(T element)
Invoking x.compareTo(y) returns < 0 (if x is less than y),
0 (if x equals y), or > 0 (if x is greater than y).
To make a class comparable, it must implement the compareTo method.

slides.title: Comparing Search Algorithms

blocks.text: For linear search, the worst case occurs when the target is not found or is the last element in the list. We should search n elements and the time complexity is O(n).
On average, the target can be in the middle of the array, and we have to search n / 2 elements. The complexity is O(n).
For binary search, the worst case is log2n comparisons and the time complexity is O(log n).
Binary search is much faster for large values of n. However, binary search works only if the array is sorted.

slides.title: Sorting

blocks.text: Sorting is the process of arranging a group of items into a defined order based on a particular criteria.
Ascending order: small to large
Descending order: large to small
Many sorting algorithms have been designed
Sequential sorts typically require n2 comparisons to sort n elements
Logarithmic sorts typically require n log2 n comparisons.
As with searching, sorting must compare generic elements.

slides.title: Selection Sort

blocks.text: Selection sort orders an array by selecting the next smallest element and putting it into its final sorted position.
The Selection Sort algorithm works as follows:
Find the smallest element in the array
Switch it with the element in the first position
Find the next smallest element in the array
Switch it with the element in the next position
Repeat until all elements are in their proper places

slides.title: Insertion Sort

blocks.text: Insertion sort orders an array by repeatedly inserting a new element into a subset that has already been sorted.
The Insertion Sort algorithm works as follows:
Start at the second array element.
Insert the second element into the proper position shifting the first element if needed.
Insert the third element into the sorted subarray, shifting the first two elements if needed.
Repeat until all array elements have been inserted properly.

Bubble Sort

blocks.text: Bubble sort orders an array by comparing neighboring elements and swapping their positions if necessary.
The Bubble Sort algorithm works as follows:
Traverse the array, exchanging adjacent elements if they are not in their relative order.
After the first pass, the highest value is moved to the end of array
Traverse the array again, moving the second highest value
Repeat until all elements have been placed in their proper order

slides.title: Quick Sort

blocks.text: Quick sort orders values by partitioning an array around one pivot element, then sorting each partition.
The Quick Sort algorithm works as follows:
Choose one element in the array to be the pivot element. The choice is arbitrary. We will choose the rightmost element as pivot.
Partition the array so that all elements less than the pivot element go to the left and all elements greater than or equal go to the right.
Apply the quick sort algorithm recursively to both partitions.
The algorithm works regardless of our choice of the pivot.

Merge Sort

blocks.text: Merge sort orders values by recursively dividing the array in half until each subarray has only one element, then merging the subarrays recursively to become a sorted array.
The Merge Sort algorithm works as follows:
Recursively divide the array into roughly two equal subarrays.
Continue dividing until each subarray has only one element.
Merge two subarrays into a sorted subarray.
Continue merging recursively to have a complete sorted array.

Comparing Sort Algorithms

blocks.text: The selection sort, insertion sort, and bubble sort algorithms are relatively simple but use two nested loops.
They require about n2 comparisons.
Their time complexity is O(n2).
The merge sort algorithm divides the array repeatedly in half, resulting in log2 n number of levels for merging.
The time to merge n elements at each level is O(n).
Therefore, the time complexity of merge sort is O(n log n).

If the partitioning of elements is balanced and divides the subarray elements into nearly two equal halves, then the depth of partitioning is O(log2 n) levels.
However, if the partitioning of elements is unbalanced around the pivot, then the number of levels becomes O(n).
The average time complexity of quick sort is O(n log n).
However, the worst-case complexity of quick sort is O(n2).

slides.title: Radix Sort

blocks.text: All the sorting algorithms we have discussed so far compare the elements to each other. The best was O(n log n).
Can we sort an array without comparing elements?
A sort algorithm is typically based on some key value.
For example, we can sort people based on their ID or last name.
To sort integer IDs, we can group the numbers according to
10 possible digits (0 to 9). The radix is 10.
To sort by last name, we can group the strings according to
26 possible letters. The radix becomes 26.

slides.title: Radix Sort Algorithm

blocks.text: Radix sort makes multiple passes through an integer array.
In the first pass, it sorts the array based on digits in the unit position (rightmost digit of each number).
In the second pass, it sorts the array based on digits in the 10s position (weight = 10).
In the third pass, it sorts the array based on digits in the 100s position (weight = 100).
After completing all passes, the integer array becomes sorted.

Analysis of Radix Sort

blocks.text: Radix sort is a non-comparative sorting algorithm that sorts the integer keys according to their digit values.
Unlike the comparative sorting algorithms discussed earlier, radix sort is not a generic algorithm.
The time complexity of radix sort is O(d × n), where d is the number of digits (passes), and n is the number of elements.
If d is a constant and n is large, then O(d × n) = O(n).
For large n, radix sort is faster than quick sort and merge sort. However, it is less efficient for small n.
